summary: The big brown goose with a black neck and white chinstrap — the park's most obvious waterbird.
idTips: Black head and long black neck with a white 'chinstrap' running under the chin.
Gray-brown body, paler chest, white under the tail.
Flies in V-shaped or wavering lines, honking.

lookAlikes.name: Cackling Goose
lookAlikes.howToTell: Rare in the park. Mallard-sized with a stubby bill and short neck; Canada Goose is far larger with a long, sloping bill.

whereInPark: The Reservoir, Harlem Meer, the Lake, and the open lawns where they graze.
whenInPark: Year-round; numbers rise in fall and winter when migrants join the local birds.
behavior: Grazes on lawns in family groups. Hisses and lowers its head when approached — give goslings space in spring.
voice: A deep, two-part honk (ha-ronk), often from many birds at once.

summary: A small, crested duck; the male is arguably the most ornate bird in the park.
idTips: Male: glossy green crested head with crisp white face stripes, red eye, chestnut breast.
Female: gray-brown with a white teardrop-shaped patch around the eye and a subtle crest.
Often sits under overhanging branches along the shore rather than out on open water.

lookAlikes.name: Mandarin Duck
lookAlikes.howToTell: An escaped Asian species (one became famous at the Pond in 2018). Male has orange 'sails' on the back and orange whisker plumes; female has a thin white line behind the eye instead of a teardrop.

whereInPark: Quiet coves of the Lake along the Ramble shore, the Pool in the North Woods, and Harlem Meer.
whenInPark: Small numbers most of the year; easiest to find in spring and fall.
behavior: Shy. Swims close to shoreline cover and flushes with a squeal. Perches on branches — unusual for a duck.
voice: Female gives a rising, squealing oo-eek when flushed; male a thin, high whistle.

summary: A duck with an oversized, spoon-shaped bill that feeds by spinning in circles.
idTips: Huge, broad, spatula-shaped bill — longer than the head — is the giveaway at any distance.
Male: green head, white chest, rusty-chestnut sides, yellow eye.
Female: mottled brown like a female Mallard, but with that enormous bill.

lookAlikes.name: Mallard
lookAlikes.howToTell: Male Mallard also has a green head, but a chestnut breast (not white) and a normal-sized yellow bill. Females differ mainly in bill shape.

whereInPark: The Reservoir — rafts of shovelers gather there through the winter.
whenInPark: October to April, peaking in late fall and winter. Rare in summer.
behavior: Groups swim in tight circles with bills skimming the surface, stirring up food and filtering it.
voice: Usually quiet; males give a soft, hollow took-took.

summary: The classic park duck — the starting point for learning every other duck.
idTips: Male: glossy green head, thin white neck ring, chestnut breast, gray body, yellow bill.
Female: mottled brown with an orange-and-dark bill.
Both show a blue wing patch (the speculum) edged in white.

lookAlikes.name: American Black Duck
lookAlikes.howToTell: Darker, chocolate-brown all over with a paler face; wing patch is purple-blue without white edges. Hybrids with Mallards are common.

lookAlikes.name: Northern Shoveler
lookAlikes.howToTell: Look at the bill: a shoveler's is huge and spoon-shaped.

whereInPark: Every water body — the Pond, the Lake, Turtle Pond, Harlem Meer, and the Reservoir.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Dabbles — tips tail-up to feed rather than diving. Readily approaches people (please don't feed bread).
voice: The female gives the classic loud quack; males make a softer, raspy note.

summary: A tiny, round diving duck with a big white head patch.
idTips: Male: mostly white body with a black back; dark head with a large white wedge behind the eye.
Female: gray-brown with a neat white oval on the cheek.
Dives constantly and pops back up like a cork.

lookAlikes.name: Hooded Merganser
lookAlikes.howToTell: Male also has a white head patch, but it's fan-shaped and outlined in black, with rusty sides and a thin bill.

whereInPark: The Reservoir; occasionally Harlem Meer.
whenInPark: November to April.
behavior: Small groups dive in unison; one bird often stays up as a lookout.
voice: Mostly silent.

summary: A compact, stiff-tailed diving duck that often naps with its tail cocked up.
idTips: Winter male: gray-brown body, dark cap, bright white cheek.
Female: similar, but with a dark line across the pale cheek.
Stiff, spiky tail often held upright.

lookAlikes.name: Bufflehead
lookAlikes.howToTell: Bufflehead's white is behind the eye on a dark head; Ruddy's white fills the whole cheek below a dark cap.

whereInPark: The Reservoir, often in large rafts.
whenInPark: November to April.
behavior: Spends much of the day asleep on the water; dives rather than flies to escape.
voice: Silent in winter.

summary: The city pigeon — worth a second look for its surprising variety.
idTips: Classic bird: blue-gray with two black bars on each wing and an iridescent green-purple neck.
White rump shows in flight on the classic pattern.
Colors vary widely — checkered, white, reddish-brown — all the same species.

lookAlikes.name: Mourning Dove
lookAlikes.howToTell: Slimmer and tan-brown, with a long pointed tail and black spots on the wings.

whereInPark: Plazas, lawns, and around park entrances.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Feeds on the ground in flocks; males puff up and turn in circles while cooing at females.
voice: Soft, throaty coos.

summary: A slim, soft-brown dove with a long pointed tail.
idTips: Plain tan-buff body, small round head, black spots on the wing.
Long, pointed tail with white edges shows in flight.
Wings make a whistling sound on takeoff.

lookAlikes.name: Rock Pigeon
lookAlikes.howToTell: Chunkier and gray, with a short, square tail.

whereInPark: Lawns, path edges, and the winter feeders in the Ramble.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Picks seeds from the ground; often sits on branches in pairs.
voice: A mournful coo-OOO-oo-oo-oo, often mistaken for an owl.

summary: The medium-sized gull of lawns and the Reservoir — learn it first, then compare other gulls to it.
idTips: Adult: pale gray back, white head and body, yellow bill with a crisp black ring near the tip.
Yellowish legs.
Young birds are mottled brown-gray and take about three years to look like adults.

lookAlikes.name: Herring Gull
lookAlikes.howToTell: Noticeably bigger, with pink legs and a red spot (not a black ring) on the yellow bill.

whereInPark: The Reservoir, the Great Lawn, Sheep Meadow, and any open water.
whenInPark: Most of the year; most numerous fall through spring.
behavior: Loafs on lawns and open water; scavenges boldly around people.
voice: High-pitched mewing and laughing calls.

summary: A large black waterbird that swims low and dries its wings spread wide.
idTips: All dark, with a long neck and hooked bill; orange-yellow skin at the base of the bill.
Swims with the body low in the water and the bill angled slightly upward.
Perches with wings held open to dry.

lookAlikes.name: Great Cormorant
lookAlikes.howToTell: Rare in the park, mostly in winter. Bigger and bulkier with a white throat patch; young birds have a white belly.

whereInPark: The Reservoir, the Lake, and Harlem Meer; look for birds drying on rocks and snags.
whenInPark: Mostly April to November.
behavior: Dives from the surface and stays under for long stretches, popping up yards away.
voice: Silent away from nesting colonies.

summary: The park's tallest bird — a big blue-gray heron.
idTips: Very tall and blue-gray, with a long, dagger-like bill.
White face with a black stripe over the eye that ends in plumes.
In flight: slow, deep wingbeats with the neck folded back.

lookAlikes.name: Great Egret
lookAlikes.howToTell: All white rather than blue-gray.

whereInPark: Turtle Pond, the Lake, the Pool, and Harlem Meer.
whenInPark: Seen in every season; most often in spring and fall.
behavior: Hunts by standing still for long periods; flies off with a deep croak if disturbed.
voice: A deep, harsh, prehistoric-sounding croak.

summary: A tall, all-white heron with a yellow bill and black legs.
idTips: All white, very tall and slender, with an S-curved neck.
Yellow bill; black legs and feet.
Flies with the neck tucked in and legs trailing.

lookAlikes.name: Snowy Egret
lookAlikes.howToTell: Smaller, with a black bill and bright yellow feet ('golden slippers').

whereInPark: Turtle Pond, the Lake, and Harlem Meer — anywhere with shallow edges.
whenInPark: April to October.
behavior: Stands motionless or stalks slowly in shallow water, then strikes at fish with a lightning jab.
voice: A low, harsh croak when disturbed.

summary: A stocky, short-necked heron that roosts by day in shoreline trees.
idTips: Adult: black cap and back, pale gray wings, white underparts, red eye.
Juvenile: brown with heavy white spots and streaks — it looks like a different bird.
Hunched posture with the neck pulled in; looks almost neckless at rest.

lookAlikes.name: Green Heron
lookAlikes.howToTell: Much smaller, with a dark green back and chestnut neck.

lookAlikes.name: Yellow-crowned Night Heron
lookAlikes.howToTell: Juveniles are similar; Yellow-crowned is grayer with finer spots and a thicker, all-dark bill. Adults have a black-and-white striped face.

whereInPark: Shorelines of the Lake, Turtle Pond, and Harlem Meer, often perched in overhanging branches.
whenInPark: Mostly March to November; a few remain in winter.
behavior: Most active at dusk and night. By day it roosts quietly and is easy to walk right past.
voice: A single flat, barking quok, often heard overhead at dusk.

summary: Central Park's famous resident hawk, often perched high or soaring over the lawns.
idTips: Adult has a brick-red tail — visible from above, or from below when the light shines through.
Pale chest with a band of dark streaks across the belly (the 'belly band').
From below, a dark bar along the leading edge of the inner wing.

lookAlikes.name: Cooper's Hawk
lookAlikes.howToTell: Smaller and slimmer with a long, banded tail and short rounded wings; flies with quick flaps and glides through trees rather than soaring in wide circles.

whereInPark: Anywhere — scan tall trees, the building tops along Fifth Avenue and Central Park West, the Great Lawn, Turtle Pond, and the North End.
whenInPark: Year-round; pairs have nested in and around the park for decades.
behavior: Hunts rats and squirrels from a high perch; soars on broad wings with a fanned tail.
voice: A hoarse, descending scream (kee-eeer) — the 'hawk cry' movies use for every raptor.

summary: A shaggy-crested, blue-gray bird that plunges headfirst for fish.
idTips: Big head with a ragged crest and a heavy, dagger-like bill.
Blue-gray above, with a blue band across the white chest.
Female has an extra rusty-orange band across the belly — one of few birds where the female is more colorful.

lookAlikes.name: Blue Jay
lookAlikes.howToTell: Jays are bright blue with black-and-white wings and a neat crest, and they don't hover or dive into water.

whereInPark: The Lake, Harlem Meer, the Pool, and Turtle Pond — listen for the rattle.
whenInPark: Mostly in migration and winter; scarce in summer.
behavior: Perches over water or hovers, then dives headfirst; flies low and fast along the shore.
voice: A loud, dry rattle — often the first clue that one is around.

summary: A common, noisy woodpecker with a zebra-barred back and a red head — the red belly is barely visible.
idTips: Black-and-white 'zebra' barring across the back.
Male: red from bill to nape. Female: red only on the nape.
Pale gray-buff face and underparts; the namesake reddish wash on the belly is faint.

lookAlikes.name: Red-headed Woodpecker
lookAlikes.howToTell: Uncommon. Entire head is deep red, with a solid black back and big white wing patches — no barring.

lookAlikes.name: Northern Flicker
lookAlikes.howToTell: Brown and spotted below with a black chest crescent; often on the ground.

whereInPark: Woodlands throughout — the Ramble, the North Woods, Hallett Nature Sanctuary — and at feeders.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Hitches up trunks and big limbs; wedges nuts into bark crevices to store them.
voice: A rolling kwirr and a loud chiff-chiff.

summary: A quiet woodpecker that drills neat rows of sap wells in tree bark.
idTips: Long white stripe along the folded wing — the best field mark.
Red forehead; male also has a red throat (female's is white).
Look for horizontal rows of small holes on trunks — its sap wells.

lookAlikes.name: Downy Woodpecker
lookAlikes.howToTell: Smaller, with a white stripe down the back instead of along the wing, and no red on the forehead.

whereInPark: Woodlands across the park; check trees with fresh rows of sap wells.
whenInPark: Mostly April and October; some stay the winter.
behavior: Clings quietly at its sap wells, returning to sip sap and eat the insects drawn to it.
voice: A nasal, mewing neeah; drums in an irregular, stuttering rhythm.

summary: The smallest and most common woodpecker, often traveling with chickadees.
idTips: Black and white with a broad white stripe down the back.
Tiny bill, much shorter than the head.
Male has a small red patch on the back of the head.

lookAlikes.name: Hairy Woodpecker
lookAlikes.howToTell: Bigger, with a bill about as long as its head (Downy's is stubby). Outer tail feathers plain white; Downy's have black spots.

whereInPark: Anywhere with trees — even weed stems and shrubs — plus the Ramble feeders.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Forages on thin branches and weed stems, often upside down.
voice: A soft pik and a descending, whinnying rattle.

summary: A larger, longer-billed version of the Downy — the classic ID test for new birders.
idTips: Bill about as long as the head — the key difference from Downy.
Same black-and-white pattern, with a white back stripe.
Clean white outer tail feathers without black spots.

lookAlikes.name: Downy Woodpecker
lookAlikes.howToTell: Downy is smaller with a stubby bill and black spots on the white outer tail.

whereInPark: Larger trees in the Ramble and the North Woods.
whenInPark: Year-round, less common than Downy.
behavior: Works trunks and large limbs, hammering harder than a Downy.
voice: A loud, sharp peek and a fast rattle on one pitch.

summary: A big, brown woodpecker that feeds on the ground for ants.
idTips: Brown barred back, spotted belly, and a black crescent on the chest.
Bright white rump and yellow underwings flash in flight.
Male has a black 'mustache'; both sexes have a red patch on the nape.

lookAlikes.name: Red-bellied Woodpecker
lookAlikes.howToTell: Zebra-barred back and no black chest crescent; rarely feeds on the ground.

whereInPark: Lawns and meadow edges — the Great Hill, the North Meadow, and around Sheep Meadow in migration.
whenInPark: Small numbers year-round; many more in fall migration (September–October).
behavior: Hops on lawns probing for ants; flies up into trees with a bounding flight.
voice: A loud, long wick-wick-wick-wick and a single piercing klee-yer.

summary: A plain gray-brown flycatcher that constantly pumps its tail.
idTips: Dark head, gray-brown back, whitish underparts; no bold wingbars.
Pumps and fans its tail downward while perched.
All-dark bill.

lookAlikes.name: Eastern Wood-Pewee
lookAlikes.howToTell: Has two clear wingbars and a pale lower bill, and doesn't wag its tail; arrives later, in mid-May.

whereInPark: Low perches near water — the Pool, the Lake shore, and Turtle Pond.
whenInPark: One of the first spring migrants (late March–April); again in October.
behavior: Sallies out from a low perch to snap up insects, then returns to the same spot.
voice: Says its name: a raspy fee-bee.

summary: A bold, crested, blue-and-white jay with a big vocabulary.
idTips: Bright blue above with a crest; white face and underparts.
Black necklace across the throat and chest.
White patches and black bars on the blue wings and tail.

lookAlikes.name: Belted Kingfisher
lookAlikes.howToTell: Kingfisher is blue-gray with a huge bill and shaggy crest, and lives along the water.

whereInPark: Woodlands throughout; noisy at the Ramble feeders.
whenInPark: Year-round; big migrating flocks pass over in late September–October and in May.
behavior: Caches acorns. Mobs hawks and owls — follow screaming jays to find raptors.
voice: A loud jay-jay scream, squeaky gate calls, and a convincing Red-tailed Hawk imitation.

summary: The all-black, intelligent crow of lawns and treetops.
idTips: Entirely glossy black, including bill and legs.
Square or slightly rounded tail in flight.
Walks confidently on lawns.

lookAlikes.name: Fish Crow
lookAlikes.howToTell: Nearly identical to look at; the reliable difference is voice — a nasal, short uh-uh instead of a clear caw.

lookAlikes.name: Common Grackle
lookAlikes.howToTell: Much smaller, with a long keel-shaped tail and a pale yellow eye.

whereInPark: Lawns, treetops, and the sky over the whole park.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Forages on the ground in pairs or families; mobs hawks loudly.
voice: A clear, familiar caw-caw.

summary: A tiny, curious bird with a black cap and bib — the core of winter mixed flocks.
idTips: Black cap and black bib with bright white cheeks.
Soft gray back and buffy sides.
Tiny bill; acrobatic, often hangs upside down.

lookAlikes.name: Carolina Chickadee
lookAlikes.howToTell: Very rare this far north. Nearly identical; Black-capped shows whiter edges on the wing feathers and a raggeder lower edge to the bib. Song is the best clue.

whereInPark: The Ramble, the North Woods, and the feeders; listen for it in any mixed flock.
whenInPark: Year-round; numbers vary from year to year.
behavior: Travels in small flocks with titmice, nuthatches, and kinglets — find the chickadees and you've found the flock.
voice: Says chick-a-dee-dee-dee; the song is a clear, whistled fee-bee.

summary: A small gray bird with a pointed crest and big dark eyes.
idTips: Soft gray above, whitish below, with peachy-orange flanks.
Pointed gray crest.
Small black patch just above the bill.

lookAlikes.name: Black-capped Chickadee
lookAlikes.howToTell: Chickadee has a black cap and bib, and no crest.

whereInPark: Woodlands and feeders throughout the park.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Bold and noisy; holds seeds with its feet and hammers them open.
voice: A loud, whistled peter-peter-peter.

summary: A tiny, restless olive bird that constantly flicks its wings.
idTips: Olive-gray with a broken white eye ring and a white wingbar.
Nervous wing-flicking — it's almost never still.
Male's red crown patch is usually hidden; it flares when the bird is excited.

lookAlikes.name: Golden-crowned Kinglet
lookAlikes.howToTell: Has a bold black-and-white striped face and a yellow-orange crown that's always visible.

whereInPark: Thickets and woodland edges throughout — the Ramble, Shakespeare Garden, Strawberry Fields.
whenInPark: Migration: April and October–November; a few winter.
behavior: Hovers briefly to pick insects off leaf tips.
voice: A husky ji-dit call; a surprisingly loud, rollicking song for its size.

summary: One of the smallest birds in the park, with a bright striped crown.
idTips: Black-and-white striped face.
Crown stripe yellow (female) or yellow with an orange center (male).
Olive-gray body with a white wingbar.

lookAlikes.name: Ruby-crowned Kinglet
lookAlikes.howToTell: Plain face with a white eye ring, and no stripes.

whereInPark: Conifers and woodland — the pines around the Ramble and the North Woods.
whenInPark: Migration (late March–April and October–November); small numbers winter.
behavior: Forages high in conifers, constantly moving and hovering.
voice: A very high, thin see-see-see — too high for some people to hear.

summary: A sleek, crested bird with a black mask that travels in flocks looking for fruit.
idTips: Silky tan-brown with a crest and a narrow black mask.
Yellow tip to the tail.
Red, waxy tips on some wing feathers (hence the name).

lookAlikes.name: Bohemian Waxwing
lookAlikes.howToTell: Very rare here. Grayer and larger, with a rusty undertail and white-and-yellow wing marks.

whereInPark: Fruiting trees and shrubs anywhere; in summer, catching insects over the Lake and Turtle Pond.
whenInPark: Can appear in any season; flock movements are irregular.
behavior: Moves in tight flocks; birds sometimes pass berries beak to beak.
voice: Very high, thin, buzzy whistles — listen for it overhead.

summary: A blue-gray bird that walks headfirst down tree trunks.
idTips: Blue-gray back, white face and breast, black cap.
Long, slightly upturned bill.
Rusty patch under the tail.

lookAlikes.name: Red-breasted Nuthatch
lookAlikes.howToTell: Smaller, with a black eye-line, white eyebrow, and rusty-orange underparts. Irruptive — common some falls, absent in others.

whereInPark: Mature trees across the park and the Ramble feeders.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Creeps headfirst down trunks; wedges seeds into bark and hacks them open.
voice: A nasal yank-yank, like a toy horn.

summary: A tiny, bark-colored bird that spirals up tree trunks.
idTips: Streaky brown above — perfectly camouflaged against bark.
White underparts and a thin, down-curved bill.
Uses its stiff tail as a prop.

lookAlikes.name: White-breasted Nuthatch
lookAlikes.howToTell: Nuthatch is gray with a black cap and climbs down headfirst; creepers climb up.

whereInPark: Large trees in the Ramble, the North Woods, and around the Reservoir.
whenInPark: Migration and winter, roughly October to April.
behavior: Hitches up a trunk, then flies to the base of the next tree and starts again.
voice: A very high, thin seee.

summary: A small, rich-brown wren with a very loud song.
idTips: Warm rusty-brown above, buffy-orange below.
Bold white eyebrow stripe.
Often cocks its tail up.

lookAlikes.name: House Wren
lookAlikes.howToTell: Plainer gray-brown with only a faint eyebrow; mainly a spring and fall migrant here.

whereInPark: Dense undergrowth in the Ramble, the North Woods, and Hallett Nature Sanctuary.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Skulks low in tangles; pairs stay together all year.
voice: A ringing teakettle-teakettle-teakettle, far louder than you'd expect.

summary: A slate-gray bird that mews like a cat from dense shrubs.
idTips: Uniform slate gray with a black cap.
Rusty patch under the tail.
Long tail, often flicked or cocked.

lookAlikes.name: Northern Mockingbird
lookAlikes.howToTell: Paler gray with big white patches in the wings and tail.

whereInPark: Shrubby edges everywhere — the Ramble, Strawberry Fields, the North Woods.
whenInPark: Late April through October, and it nests in the park. A few try to overwinter.
behavior: Stays low in thick cover; curious and often pops out when you pish.
voice: A cat-like mew, and a long, jumbled song of squeaks and borrowed phrases.

summary: A long-tailed gray songbird famous for its endless mimicry.
idTips: Pale gray above, whitish below.
Large white wing patches and white outer tail feathers flash in flight.
Long tail; often perches conspicuously on top of shrubs.

lookAlikes.name: Gray Catbird
lookAlikes.howToTell: Darker slate gray with a black cap and no white patches.

whereInPark: Open areas with shrubs, mostly around the park's edges and the south end.
whenInPark: Year-round in small numbers.
behavior: Sings from high perches, even at night in spring; defends fruiting shrubs in winter.
voice: Long runs of other birds' songs, each phrase repeated several times.

summary: A stocky, short-tailed bird from Europe, first released in North America right here in Central Park in 1890.
idTips: Short, square tail and pointed triangular wings in flight.
Breeding: glossy purple-green with a yellow bill.
Winter: covered in white spots, with a dark bill.

lookAlikes.name: Common Grackle
lookAlikes.howToTell: Grackle has a long tail and a pale eye; starlings look short-tailed and walk with a waddling strut.

whereInPark: Lawns everywhere, especially the Great Lawn and Sheep Meadow.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Probes lawns in flocks; mimics other birds and mechanical sounds.
voice: A jumble of whistles, clicks, and imitations.

summary: A brown, spotted thrush with a reddish tail and an ethereal song.
idTips: Brown back contrasting with a warmer, reddish tail.
Spotted breast and a thin white eye ring.
Slowly raises its tail and lowers it again.

lookAlikes.name: Wood Thrush
lookAlikes.howToTell: Bigger and plumper, rusty-brown on the head and back, with large round black spots on a white breast.

lookAlikes.name: Swainson's Thrush
lookAlikes.howToTell: Evenly olive-brown with no tail contrast, and a buffy 'spectacled' eye ring.

whereInPark: Leaf litter and low branches in the Ramble and the North Woods.
whenInPark: April and October–November migration; some winter.
behavior: Hops on the forest floor flicking leaves, then freezes.
voice: A soft chuck call; the song (rarely heard here) is a flute-like phrase repeated on different pitches.

summary: The familiar orange-breasted thrush — and the size yardstick for other birds.
idTips: Brick-orange breast, gray-brown back, dark head.
Broken white eye ring and a yellow bill.
Runs and stops on lawns with its head cocked.

lookAlikes.name: Eastern Towhee
lookAlikes.howToTell: Smaller, with a black (male) or brown (female) hood and a white belly; rusty only on the sides.

whereInPark: Lawns everywhere; in winter, flocks gather in fruiting trees.
whenInPark: Year-round; most numerous in spring and fall migration.
behavior: Pulls earthworms from lawns; winter flocks switch to berries.
voice: A caroling cheerily, cheer-up, cheerio at dawn; sharp tut-tut calls.

summary: The chunky, chirping sparrow of plazas and food carts — introduced from Europe.
idTips: Male: gray crown, chestnut nape, black bib, whitish cheeks.
Female: plain buffy-brown with a pale stripe behind the eye.
Thick, conical bill and an unstreaked breast.

lookAlikes.name: White-throated Sparrow
lookAlikes.howToTell: Striped head with a white throat and a yellow spot by the eye; scratches in leaf litter in the woods rather than hopping on plazas.

lookAlikes.name: Song Sparrow
lookAlikes.howToTell: Heavily streaked breast with a central spot; House Sparrows have plain breasts.

whereInPark: Park entrances, playgrounds, plazas, and food stands.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Noisy flocks dust-bathe and hop around people.
voice: Monotonous cheep-cheep chirping.

summary: A small finch; males have a red head and breast, females are streaky brown.
idTips: Male: red (sometimes orange or yellow) on the head, breast, and rump.
Blurry brown streaks on the flanks and belly.
Female: plain face, streaked all over.

lookAlikes.name: Purple Finch
lookAlikes.howToTell: Male looks dipped in raspberry juice, including back and wings, with clean unstreaked flanks. Female has a bold face pattern with a white eyebrow.

whereInPark: Plantings near park entrances, edges, and feeders.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Small flocks feed on seeds and buds; males sing from treetops.
voice: A long, warbled song often ending in a burry note; a cheep call.

summary: A small finch; breeding males are brilliant lemon-yellow with a black cap.
idTips: Summer male: bright yellow with a black forehead and black-and-white wings.
Winter: dull brownish-olive with a buffy face, but always bold wingbars.
Bouncy, roller-coaster flight.

lookAlikes.name: Yellow Warbler
lookAlikes.howToTell: All yellow with no black cap or black wings, and a thin, pointed bill.

lookAlikes.name: Pine Siskin
lookAlikes.howToTell: Heavily streaked brown with yellow flashes in the wings; irruptive.

whereInPark: Weedy edges, gardens such as the Conservatory Garden and Shakespeare Garden, and feeders.
whenInPark: Year-round; numbers vary.
behavior: Clings to seedheads like coneflower and thistle; forms flocks in winter.
voice: In flight, a cheerful per-chick-o-ree or po-ta-to-chip.

summary: A slate-gray sparrow with a white belly that arrives with winter.
idTips: Slate-gray hood and back with a clean white belly.
Pale pinkish bill.
White outer tail feathers flash as it flies off.

lookAlikes.name: Eastern Towhee
lookAlikes.howToTell: Bigger, with rusty sides and white wing patches; male black, female brown.

whereInPark: Path edges, lawns along woodland borders, and the Ramble feeders.
whenInPark: Late October to April.
behavior: Feeds on the ground in loose flocks, often with White-throated Sparrows.
voice: A sharp tick and a dry, musical trill.

summary: Central Park's signature winter sparrow, scratching in leaves everywhere.
idTips: Crisp white throat patch outlined in gray.
Yellow spot between the eye and the bill.
Striped head: white-striped and tan-striped forms both occur.

lookAlikes.name: White-crowned Sparrow
lookAlikes.howToTell: No white throat or yellow spot; pinkish-orange bill and gray neck. Uncommon in the park.

whereInPark: Leaf litter and brushy edges throughout — the Ramble, the North Woods, everywhere in fall.
whenInPark: Fall through spring, roughly October to mid-May; absent in summer.
behavior: Double-scratch hops in dead leaves, kicking back with both feet.
voice: A clear, whistled Old Sam Peabody-Peabody-Peabody (or Oh sweet Canada-Canada).

summary: A streaky brown sparrow with a central breast spot and a busy song.
idTips: Heavy brown streaks on a white breast, converging in a central spot.
Gray-and-brown striped face with a dark 'mustache' stripe.
Pumps its long, rounded tail in flight.

lookAlikes.name: Savannah Sparrow
lookAlikes.howToTell: Shorter-tailed, with a yellow spot over the eye and finer streaks; on lawns in migration.

lookAlikes.name: Lincoln's Sparrow
lookAlikes.howToTell: Finer, crisper streaks on a buffy chest and a gray face; more secretive.

whereInPark: Brushy edges near water — Turtle Pond, Harlem Meer, the Pool.
whenInPark: Most of the year; most numerous in March–April and October.
behavior: Sings from exposed perches; ducks into cover when disturbed.
voice: Two or three clear notes, then a jumbled trill: maids-maids-maids, put on your tea-kettle-ettle-ettle.

summary: A big, striking sparrow that scratches noisily in dead leaves.
idTips: Male: black hood and back. Female: warm brown instead of black.
Rusty-orange sides and a white belly.
Red eye; white corners on the long tail.

lookAlikes.name: American Robin
lookAlikes.howToTell: Robin's whole breast is orange, with no dark hood or white belly.

whereInPark: Thick undergrowth in the Ramble and the North Woods.
whenInPark: Migration (April and October); a few winter.
behavior: Hops backward to scratch through leaf litter — often heard before it's seen.
voice: A rising chewink call; the song is drink-your-teeeee.

summary: A flame-orange-and-black songbird of the treetops in May.
idTips: Male: black hood and back, brilliant orange underparts and rump.
Female: yellow-orange below, olive-brown above, with two white wingbars.
Sharp, pointed, silver-gray bill.

lookAlikes.name: Orchard Oriole
lookAlikes.howToTell: Smaller; adult male is deep chestnut (not orange) and black. Females are greenish-yellow.

lookAlikes.name: American Robin
lookAlikes.howToTell: Robin's orange is a duller brick color, and it lacks the black hood and white wingbars.

whereInPark: Tall trees across the park; in May, check the treetops around the Ramble.
whenInPark: Arrives late April–May and some stay to nest; gone by September.
behavior: Weaves a hanging, sock-shaped nest high on a drooping branch.
voice: Rich, flute-like whistled phrases and a dry chatter.

summary: The male's red-and-yellow shoulder patches are a sure sign of spring at the park's ponds.
idTips: Male: glossy black with red shoulder patches edged in yellow.
Female: heavily streaked brown — easily mistaken for a big sparrow.
Sharp, pointed bill.

lookAlikes.name: Common Grackle
lookAlikes.howToTell: Larger and iridescent, with a long tail and a pale eye; no red shoulders.

lookAlikes.name: Song Sparrow
lookAlikes.howToTell: Female blackbirds are larger and darker, with a longer, pointier bill.

whereInPark: Reeds and shoreline plants at Turtle Pond, Harlem Meer, and the Pool.
whenInPark: Arrives in March; most visible March–July and in migration.
behavior: Males flare their shoulders and sing from cattails to defend territory.
voice: A gurgling conk-la-reee.

summary: A long-tailed, iridescent blackbird with piercing pale eyes.
idTips: Long, keel-shaped tail.
Glossy purple-blue head and bronze body in good light.
Pale yellow eye.

lookAlikes.name: European Starling
lookAlikes.howToTell: Starling is short-tailed with a dark eye.

lookAlikes.name: American Crow
lookAlikes.howToTell: Much bigger and flat black, with a dark eye.

whereInPark: Lawns and pond edges throughout.
whenInPark: Mostly March to October; large flocks in migration, a few in winter.
behavior: Struts on lawns; raids nests and will even catch small birds.
voice: A harsh, squeaky readle-eak, like a rusty gate.

summary: A zebra-striped warbler that creeps along trunks like a nuthatch.
idTips: Bold black-and-white stripes all over, including the crown.
Creeps up, down, and around trunks and branches.
Male has a black throat; the female's is white.

lookAlikes.name: Blackpoll Warbler
lookAlikes.howToTell: Spring male has a solid black cap and white cheeks (not a striped crown), and doesn't creep on bark.

whereInPark: The Ramble and the North Woods during migration.
whenInPark: Migration: mid-April to May and August to October.
behavior: Forages on bark like a nuthatch — unique among warblers.
voice: A high, squeaky wheesy-wheesy-wheesy, like a squeaky wheel.

summary: A skulking warbler; the male wears a black bandit mask.
idTips: Male: broad black mask bordered above by white.
Bright yellow throat and olive back.
Female: no mask; olive with a yellow throat.

lookAlikes.name: Kentucky Warbler
lookAlikes.howToTell: Rare. Yellow 'spectacles' and all-yellow underparts, with black on the face below the eye.

whereInPark: Low, wet thickets — the Pool, the edges of Turtle Pond and Harlem Meer, the North Woods.
whenInPark: May and September–October migration.
behavior: Stays low in dense vegetation; pops up curiously when you pish.
voice: A rollicking witchety-witchety-witchety.

summary: A hyperactive warbler that fans its patterned tail to flush insects.
idTips: Male: black with bright orange patches on the wings, tail, and sides.
Female and young: gray with yellow patches in the same places.
Constantly fans its tail and droops its wings.

lookAlikes.name: Baltimore Oriole
lookAlikes.howToTell: Much bigger, with fully orange underparts rather than side patches.

whereInPark: Woodlands — the Ramble, the North Woods, and Strawberry Fields.
whenInPark: May and late August–September migration.
behavior: Flashes its colorful tail and darts after flying insects.
voice: High, variable songs, often ending in an emphatic down-slurred note: see-see-see-SEEoo.

summary: A striking warbler; the male is navy blue, black, and white.
idTips: Male: deep blue back, black face and throat, white belly.
Both sexes: a small white square on the wing (the 'pocket handkerchief').
Female: plain olive-brown with a pale eyebrow — look for that white wing square.

lookAlikes.name: Cerulean Warbler
lookAlikes.howToTell: Rare here. Sky-blue with white wingbars and a thin dark necklace, not a black face.

whereInPark: Low and mid-level in the Ramble and the North Woods.
whenInPark: May and September–October migration.
behavior: Forages in the understory, often lower than other warblers.
voice: A lazy, buzzy I'm so la-zeee, rising at the end.

summary: A tail-bobbing warbler that feeds on the ground — one of the first warblers each spring.
idTips: Constant tail-bobbing, even while walking.
Bright yellow under the tail.
Spring: rusty cap and yellow eyebrow.

lookAlikes.name: Yellow-rumped Warbler
lookAlikes.howToTell: Yellow is on the rump and the sides of the chest, not under the tail, and it doesn't bob its tail.

whereInPark: Lawns and path edges near the woods, and low in the Ramble.
whenInPark: An early migrant in April and a late one in October.
behavior: Walks on the ground or low branches, pumping its tail.
voice: A sharp chik call; the song is a buzzy trill.

summary: The most numerous warbler in migration — look for the yellow rump.
idTips: Bright yellow rump patch (birders call it 'butter butt').
Yellow patches on the sides of the chest.
Winter birds are brownish and streaked, but keep the yellow rump.

lookAlikes.name: Magnolia Warbler
lookAlikes.howToTell: Also has a yellow rump, but bright yellow underparts with black streaks and a white band across the tail.

lookAlikes.name: Palm Warbler
lookAlikes.howToTell: Yellow under the tail (not the rump), and it constantly bobs its tail.

whereInPark: Everywhere in migration; in winter, near fruiting shrubs and sunny edges.
whenInPark: April–early May and October; a few winter.
behavior: Adaptable — catches flying insects, gleans leaves, and eats berries.
voice: A sharp check call; the song is a loose, warbled trill.

summary: A spring jewel: brilliant red with black wings, high in the canopy.
idTips: Breeding male: scarlet body with jet-black wings and tail.
Female and fall male: olive-yellow with darker wings.
Stout, pale bill.

lookAlikes.name: Northern Cardinal
lookAlikes.howToTell: Cardinal has a crest, red wings, and a black face.

whereInPark: Treetops in the Ramble and the North Woods.
whenInPark: May and September migration.
behavior: Moves slowly through the canopy — surprisingly hard to spot despite the color.
voice: A burry, robin-like song and a distinctive chip-burr call.

summary: The bright red, crested songbird — a year-round park favorite.
idTips: Male: all red with a black face around a thick red-orange bill.
Female: warm tan-brown with red tinges in the wings, tail, and crest.
Pointed crest and heavy conical bill.

lookAlikes.name: Scarlet Tanager
lookAlikes.howToTell: Male is red with jet-black wings and tail, and no crest.

lookAlikes.name: Summer Tanager
lookAlikes.howToTell: All red, but with no crest or black face and a pale bill. A rare migrant.

whereInPark: Shrubby edges and feeders throughout.
whenInPark: Year-round.
behavior: Pairs stay together; males feed females during courtship.
voice: Loud, clear whistles — cheer-cheer-cheer or birdie-birdie-birdie — and a sharp chip.

summary: A chunky songbird with a huge pale bill; the male wears a rose-red bib.
idTips: Male: black and white with a triangular rose-red patch on the chest.
Female: streaky brown with a bold white eyebrow — like a giant sparrow.
Massive pale, conical bill.

lookAlikes.name: Purple Finch
lookAlikes.howToTell: Female grosbeak resembles a huge female Purple Finch but has a much bigger bill and bold white wingbars.

whereInPark: The middle and upper canopy in the Ramble and the North Woods.
whenInPark: May and September migration.
behavior: Eats seeds, buds, and insects; often sits still for long stretches.
voice: A robin-like song, often described as a robin that took voice lessons; a squeaky-sneaker eek call.
